title: Thermal Plasticity Supports Translocation of Wild Paracentrotus lividus to Recover Overexploited Populations
content:
ABSTRACT

The gonads of the purple sea urchin Paracentrotus lividus are considered a delicacy in some European countries. Combined with rising international demand, their harvesting has become unsustainable in most regions. Despite recent fishing bans and seeding programmes using juveniles reared in hatcheries, challenges such as poaching, the long time to reach marketable size and insufficient genetic variability have required alternative approaches. Translocation of adult individuals from stable populations is emerging as a solution to restore overfished stocks, but high plasticity is required to cope with novel environmental conditions. As ocean warming is the major concern for shallow-water invertebrate communities, this study addressed the effects of varying seawater temperatures on the survival, physiology and reproduction of adult P. lividus through a 28-day controlled common garden experiment. Sea urchins from upwelling-influenced northwestern Spain (stable stock; Cabo Estai, Galicia) and upwelling-independent northern Spain (depleted stock; Bay of Biscay, Basque Country) were exposed to basal and heatwave temperatures recorded at their respective locations to investigate potential thermal adaptability. Mortality was marginal and not attributable to temperature treatments in individuals from both origins, which stabilised their physiological values over time. However, most individuals in the warmest treatment showed higher activity and faster righting time, indicating some extra energy expenditure in response to warming. Despite these metabolic differences, successful fertilisation and viability of blastula-stage cells occurred regardless of origin or treatment, confirming the species' rapid thermal plasticity. Therefore, this study provides valuable information for fishery managers to support controlled translocation measures aimed at restoring sustainable sea urchin stocks in northern Spain.
